I remember that back in the 80s, when I was still deciding what I wanted to do when I grew up, there was a distinction between a "programmer" and a "systems analyst".

The systems analyst analyzed the problem that needed to be solved and designed a solution involving a computer, including system modules, inputs, outputs, etc.

💬 Blow argues software development hasn't advanced much since the early 2000s. As a game developer, I want to offer a counter point.

In the last 3 years, there have been a lot more indie games of far higher quality than we used to get. I'm thinking of the RTS space right now. The Scouring for example. We went from having nobody but Blizzard able to make something that complex to several games with outstanding performance and complexity, often with their own custom game engines that are not only working but working better than I remember wc3/sc2 working at launch.

— barbariangrunge · 20261114T00:54:36

↳ Reply to barbariangrunge

As far as the coding user experience that I have personally observed, game programming peaked with the team developing NBA Inside Drive 2004 for the Xbox.

Their workflow was:

1) Arrive at work. Get coffee. Fetch latest code from Visual Source Safe.

2) Turn on Xbox. Hit F5 to build, deploy and start debugging on target.

3) Edit and Continue C++ in debugger IDE all day on target without ever bothering to stop the game. (Yes, this took some coding discipline to maintain.)

4) Turn off Xbox and go home.

Between the Visual Studio debugger and the Whole Tomato coding assistance, it was easy to understand the code and the runtime behavior. For anything GPU-related, Microsoft Pix for Xbox gave you a scrubbable timeline of every action, every pixel, every register change in the GPU while drawing a frame.

The hardware capabilities, available libraries, and artist tools have increased tremendously since then. But, the coding experience has not. 20 years later, I'm outside of gaming and I find most people using re-run-and-printf debugging for professional development. Even locally. I don't know how anyone gets anything done.

The only significant improvements I've seen in 20 years (besides the occasional memory tracker or profiler tool) has been AI agents and reversible debuggers. Otherwise, it's all been downhill since 2004.

💬 This is the main issue:

> The open question is supply. Finding two good used phones is easy; finding a few hundred matching ones, with healthy batteries and predictable camera behaviour, would take more work. I feel increasingly confident that it’s possible.

RaspberryPies and such are commodity hardware. You can buy one, two, ten, twenty, a hundred, and it just scales along. All of those devices will, barring perhaps a few dead-on-arrival ones covered under warranty, just work out of the box.

A used smartphone will have issues which can vary from device to device, so scaling that would take a very dedicated refurbishing setup where the quirks are ironed out (and the unsalvageable ones discarded).

I would also expect that you are starting out at the other end of the bathtub curve: with new devices you will have a few that fail soon after unboxing and using them a bit, and then they will run fine for years until you start hitting the other end of the curve and wear-related faults pop up. With old cheap phones you would start out at that side of the curve, so if you buy one hundred of those, a bunch will fail at various points soon after deploying them.

The cost of that unpredictable behaviour seems high to me. So much so that I wonder if it wouldn't be cheaper to buy a lot of unsold stock of a certain type of budget smartphone from two or three years back. Those devices could run fine as long as they aren't connected to the internet directly.

I've chatted to the guy running Citronics, they provided old but working Fairphone 3 to a workshop we had at Goatmire Elixir. They try to tackle repurposing and certifying the quality of old phones. Interesting effort and well positioned for the current climate.

Thanks to Marc Lainez and his token spend we have a great Nerves system for running the Fairphone 3 by just programming Elixir. And people are flipping new (old) phones over to be put to work every week in the Nerves Discord.

We have a good UI framework in Emerge. We have media handling with Membrane. And Nerves handles the OS integration for stuff like networking. I thoroughly enjoy making up my own mobile OS for my own purposes.

I am by no means an expert at this, but starting of with a device on the Postmarket OS list and Claude, you can get a lot of these old devices working with mainline Linux and nearly all drivers.
